subject: fieldfare
title: This Songbird Defends Its Nest by Bombing Predators With Droppings

scenes.text: A 100-gram songbird has a weapon that birds of prey avoid.
The fieldfare is a big thrush of northern Europe that nests in colonies.
When a predator comes close, the neighbors attack one after another, and each one fires its droppings. Aimed.
A 1985 study put an owl near their nests. Near a colony, it took far more hits.
Enough hits foul the feathers, and a bird with fouled feathers may struggle to fly.
It works. Colony pairs raised more chicks than pairs alone. Safety in numbers, and in ammunition.

description:
The fieldfare, a thrush weighing about 100 grams, defends its nest by pelting predators with droppings.
Fieldfares breed across northern and central Europe, singly or in colonies. When a predator approaches, the birds attack it in turn, using what one study calls aimed defecation. In an experiment with a little owl (V. Haas, Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology, 1985), a predator entering a colony was hit by significantly more faeces than one near a single nest, enough that it could affect the predator's ability to fly; early-season pairs nesting in colonies also had higher nesting success than single pairs. There are reports of soiled birds of prey as large as buzzards dying after such attacks.
Smart or just disgusting? Comment below.
first_comment: In winter, fieldfares travel in flocks of more than 200. Smart defense or just disgusting?
